title: Two Talmuds
hook: the Jerusalem Talmud, from Galilee, and the Babylonian, built on the same Mishnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vilna edition, and your line: the same page everywhere. Did you and someone else get on the same page before you talked? Today, a surprise: there is more than one Talmud. Day one thousand one hundred three.

Two families get the same recipe card from a grandmother. One family stays in the old house, near the garden where the vegetables on the card actually grow. The other family moves far away, to a big city with a busy market. Years pass. Both keep cooking from the card. Both write notes in the margins, argue about the salt, add a step here and there. One day the two notebooks are laid side by side. Same card at the center of each. Very different notes around it. That's roughly what happened to the Mishnah. Today's word is the notebook that stayed close to home.
screen: `ONE RECIPE CARD.` → `TWO KITCHENS, FAR APART.` → `TWO NOTEBOOKS.`

segments.voice: Yerushalmi. It's the name for the Jerusalem Talmud, sometimes called the Talmud of the land of Israel. Here's the first surprise: despite the name, tradition places its sages not in Jerusalem but in the towns of Galilee, in the north of the land. The other Talmud is the Bavli, the Babylonian Talmud, from the academies of Babylonia, far to the east. Both start from the same Mishnah. Both add a Gemara, the discussion, mostly in Aramaic. So the bones are shared. Second, the differences show where each was made. The Yerushalmi discusses the Mishnah's farming laws, the gifts for the poor at the corners of a field, the tithes, the year the land rests. Those laws belong to the soil of the land of Israel, and the sages there lived on that soil. The Bavli, made far away, gives those farming laws much less room. Third, the feel. Some readers who move between them describe the Yerushalmi as shorter and harder, its arguments left more in outline, while the Bavli's discussions run longer and are worked over more. The Talmud this path has been reading, the one with Rashi and Tosafot around it, is the Bavli. Fourth, the Bavli keeps a hard word about itself. In tractate Sanhedrin, a sage reads a verse from Lamentations about being made to dwell in dark places, and says: that's the Talmud of Babylonia. And the Bavli prints that line on its own page, a Talmud admitting that its way of arguing can feel like walking in the dark. Two Talmuds, one Mishnah, and a family that kept both notebooks.
screen: `SAME MISHNAH, TWO PLACES.` · `FARMING LAWS STAY IN THE LAND.` · `SHORTER AND HARDER, LONGER AND WORKED.` · `THE BAVLI'S DARK PLACES.` · then, large: `TWO TALMUDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is comparing two versions of anything. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a story your family tells, one that two people tell differently. Maybe a parent tells it one way and an aunt another. Or a memory you and a friend share, but remember in different shapes. Hold both versions side by side, without picking a winner. Notice what each one keeps that the other drops. Notice where each teller was standing. Let both stay in the room with you, neither one crossed out. The bell holds the time.
Yerushalmi. The Jerusalem Talmud, made by the sages of the land of Israel, built on the same Mishnah as the Babylonian Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: two talmuds. Today, when you hear one account of something, look for the second notebook: one other version, from someone who stood somewhere else. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: In yeshivas the Babylonian Talmud is the usual text of daily learning, and the Jerusalem Talmud is also studied, especially for the agricultural laws of the land of Israel. Some study cycles move through the Yerushalmi page by page as well.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one Talmud.
what it means: two Talmuds built on the same Mishnah, one from the land of Israel, one from Babylonia.
what a scholar hears: the Yerushalmi's Gemara on the order of Seeds, where the Bavli says far less, and Sanhedrin 24a, where Lamentations 3:6 is read about the Bavli itself.

notes: The index hook said the Babylonian 'became the main one'; the script softens this to what people usually mean in a study hall. The hook line was adjusted to avoid an unsourced ranking. Please confirm.
Galilee as the home of the Yerushalmi's sages is given as 'tradition places'; please confirm (Tiberias, Sepphoris, Caesarea are usually named; not stated).
The Bavli has Gemara on Berakhot only in the order of Zeraim, and the Yerushalmi covers Zeraim; the script says 'most of those chapters'. Please confirm.
'Shorter and harder' is attributed to readers' descriptions, not stated as fact.
Sanhedrin 24a: Lamentations 3:6 applied to the Babylonian Talmud. Paraphrased; please confirm the attribution and wording.
Recipe-card hook is an analogy only; please confirm it doesn't flatten the history.

Editor: replaced the uncited count-like claim that the Bavli leaves 'most of those chapters without a Gemara' with 'gives those farming laws much less room' (voice and myth); removed 'joking' from the Sanhedrin 24a framing and the fork's 'sage in Babylonia' (the speaker there, Rabbi Yirmeyah, is not placed in Babylonia by the text); varied the practice's breath-in/breath-out pattern used on recent days.
